blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
the side or border of something is its edge

explanation.surface: Someone propping a shelf on its side and leaving it there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just joins the two parts: the abbreviation sits before the word for side.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow horizontal surface projecting from a wall or cliff serves as a shelf.

blocks.note: a stand is a position taken, as in taking a stand
harsh means hard; with the H dropped, Cockney style, hard becomes 'ard

explanation.surface: A Cockney complaining that the usual arrangement is unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'arsh signals a dropped H, the hallmark of Cockney speech, so the synonym for harsh must drop its H too.
explanation.definitionFit: Standard as an adjective means normal, regular or customary, which is exactly what usual describes.

blocks.note: hi is a casual greeting
Jack, or Jack Tar, is an old name for a sailor

explanation.surface: Pirates who say hello to a sailor and then seize him.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack for a sailor is a common crossword convention, alongside AB, TAR and RATING.
explanation.definitionFit: To hijack is to seize a vehicle and its passengers by force, holding the people aboard as captives.

blocks.note: first meaning: a cricket fielding position beside the wicketkeeper
second meaning: a fumble or mistake, letting the ball get away

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder in a particular spot spills an easy chance.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the slips stand next to the wicketkeeper to catch edges; a slip is also any small error, such as letting a catch fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Slip names both the cricket position near the keeper and a careless error, here a ball let fall.

blocks.note: first meaning: fairly or moderately, as in quite good
second meaning: attractive, good-looking

explanation.walkthrough: Fair looks like a second adverb meaning moderate, but here it is the old sense of beautiful.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb the word means moderately or to some degree; as an adjective it means attractive in appearance.

clue.text: PM a cheat, so I gathered

indicators.note: things gathered up are bunched together in no particular order, so the letters come out rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone concluding from rumours that the prime minister is a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So I gathered' reads as hearsay, but gathered is the signal to rearrange the preceding letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Taoiseach is the title of the head of government in Ireland, its equivalent of a prime minister.

indicators.note: surreal means bizarre and dreamlike, distorted out of normal order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A gallery-goer asked whether the art is pleasingly surreal and answering enthusiastically.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and reply make it sound like a conversation about a painting; the first two words supply all the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb serves as an emphatic affirmative reply, an enthusiastic way of agreeing.

indicators.note: to be written about something is to be wrapped around it, so one part encloses the other

blocks.note: to cram is to stuff full
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A boast that the finest writing is about England.
explanation.walkthrough: Stuff looks like a noun meaning material, but it is the verb, to pack tight.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of something is its finest part, the elite, like cream rising to the top of milk.

blocks.note: first meaning: Bizet's opera about a Spanish gypsy
second meaning, split in two: men who drive cars

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an opera house's chauffeurs are all men.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading, which splits the opera's title into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Carmen is Bizet's famous opera; read as car men it whimsically describes men behind the wheel.

clue.text: Country seized by thug and autocrat

indicators.note: something seized is held within the grip of what follows, tucked inside those words

blocks.note: runs across the three words

explanation.surface: A nation taken over by a brutal dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the country's history under Idi Amin, which makes the hidden answer neatly apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Uganda is an East African nation, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Design container in which kept a tropical fruit

indicators.note: a vessel in which something is kept holds it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a plan is a design
a tin is a container
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plans for a box in which to store exotic fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' that looks like part of the definition is the piece placed inside the container.
explanation.definitionFit: The plantain is a starchy banana-like fruit grown in the tropics and usually cooked before eating.

blocks.note: first meaning: a large sum of money, as in costing a fortune
second meaning: a small paper or card container

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the paper round a peppermint; mint is actually a fortune, and a packet in British slang is also a lot of money.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a packet is a large amount of money, like a mint; it is also a small package or envelope.

clue.text: Bag flimsy, splitting in the end

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: flimsy material is thin
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheap carrier bag that tore apart eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: Bag is not a sack here but the informal sense of a person's interest, as in 'not my bag'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's bag is their particular interest or speciality, which is also called their thing, as in 'not my thing'.

blocks.note: May is a month
to hem is to edge or enclose, to bound

explanation.surface: A forecast that one particular month is sure to be chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Bound reads as 'certain', but it is the verb meaning to edge or border, as a hem does.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayhem and pandemonium are synonyms, both meaning violent disorder and wild confusion.

blocks.note: first meaning: a large seabird, something with wings
second meaning: a burden one must carry, from the bird in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: A football winger lamenting the burden he has to carry.
explanation.walkthrough: Winger suggests a wide footballer, but it means a creature with wings; the Ancient Mariner had to wear the dead bird round his neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The seabird has huge wings, and since Coleridge's poem the word also means a heavy burden or curse.

clue.text: Some supermodel sent back a slipper?

indicators.note: some of something is just a part of it, so the letters come from inside the words
sending something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: A fashion model returning a pair of slippers.
explanation.walkthrough: Slipper suggests footwear, but the question mark allows it to mean something that slips along, over snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled glides or slides over snow and ice, so whimsically it is a thing that slips.

clue.text: Controlling authority in check, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: judging by the sound means going by what is heard, not by spelling

blocks.note: to rein is to hold in check, as with a horse

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an authority figure is being kept under control.
explanation.walkthrough: Rein and the answer are pronounced identically; a rein is the strap used to hold a horse in check.
explanation.definitionFit: A reign is a period of sovereign rule, the exercise of supreme power by a monarch.

clue.text: Race about done, finally — are you kidding?

indicators.note: about means around, so one part goes round the other
finally points to the last letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a rally is a motor race over public roads
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone told a race is over already, reacting with disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About done' sounds like nearly finished, but about is the instruction to wrap and done gives only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation the word expresses surprise or doubt, just like asking whether someone is joking.

clue.text: Meat, not a sausage at Lord’s?

blocks.note: first meaning: the flesh of the bird eaten as food
second meaning: a batsman's score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: A cricket ground canteen with meat on offer but no sausages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a sausage' is British slang for nothing at all, and Lord's is the London cricket ground, so this means a score of zero in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Duck is a poultry meat, and in cricket a batsman out without scoring has made a duck.

clue.text: Abominable serving of food with bad filling

indicators.note: a filling sits inside whatever surrounds it, like the middle of a sandwich

blocks.note: a dish is a serving of food
evil means bad

explanation.surface: A dreadful meal with a nasty filling.
explanation.walkthrough: Filling suggests a pie's contents, but it instructs one word to go inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish means wicked or fiendish, like the devil, and so dreadful or abominable.

blocks.note: pop and pa are both informal words for father
Ella Fitzgerald was a celebrated jazz singer

explanation.surface: Asking about a recipe belonging to a pop star named Fitzgerald.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop singer' reads as one phrase, but pop is a word for dad, leaving singer to go with Fitzgerald.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked in a wide pan with saffron, seafood or meat.

blocks.note: first meaning: a small lockable storage cabinet
second meaning, whimsical: something that locks

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a key as 'one that locks' is a playful sense rather than a dictionary one.
explanation.definitionFit: A locker is a lockable storage cupboard, as in a gym, and literally anything that locks is a locker.

blocks.note: first meaning: fashionable, excellent, in 1960s slang
second meaning: covered in grooves

explanation.surface: Praising something retro as cool, like old vinyl.
explanation.walkthrough: The slang word for cool comes from the groove of a record, so the second reading is the literal one.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixties slang word means fashionable and excellent; literally it describes a surface full of grooves, as a record has.

clue.text: Very many minions, but no leader

indicators.note: without a leader means the front is lost, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: a poodle is a servile follower or lackey

explanation.surface: A horde of underlings left without a boss.
explanation.walkthrough: A poodle, in British political slang, is someone who slavishly follows another; drop its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Oodles is an informal word for a great quantity, so it means a very large number.

clue.text: Royal meeting lucky person, cap doffed

indicators.note: doffing a cap takes off the top, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a mascot is a person or thing thought to bring good luck

explanation.surface: Someone fortunate meeting the royals and politely raising their hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Ascot is an annual horse-racing meeting in Berkshire attended by the royal family, where hats are famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Ascot is a prestigious race meeting with royal patronage, so the name is a royal meeting.

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds
let means allowed

explanation.surface: Two people permitted to wear their jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: Couple reads as two people, but here it is a pair of anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracelet is an ornamental band worn on the wrist, an item of jewellery.

indicators.note: an audio book is listened to, so the word is taken as it is heard

blocks.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: Keeping up with the plot of a recorded book.
explanation.walkthrough: Tale and the answer are pronounced the same; the audio book supplies the listening.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to follow them closely and secretly, as a detective does.

indicators.note: a new design remakes the thing in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Admiring a freshly designed coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is informal shortening of delicious, which a tasty meal might be called.
explanation.definitionFit: Delish is slang for delicious, used loosely as general praise much as lovely is.

blocks.note: as, as in 'as good', means equally
set means ready, as in ready, steady, go

explanation.surface: Everyone equally prepared to lend a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Help is a noun here, a useful resource, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful or valuable person or thing, a source of benefit or support.

blocks.note: first meaning: very quickly, without hesitation
second meaning, literal: resembling a fired round

explanation.surface: Describing something as swift as a speeding bullet, Superman style.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for doing something instantly, read literally, compares it to a fired projectile.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means immediately and very quickly; literally it likens motion to a fired bullet.
